context: Arithmetic: field of fractions of the integers, prior to constructing the real numbers
editorial_note: ProofWiki presents both fraction representations and the more structural field-of-fractions definition. Fractions are equivalence classes of integer numerator/denominator pairs, so p/q is not a unique syntactic representation. This definition is independent of the construction of R and useful for rational Cauchy sequences. The representation equality criterion can be established within Z.
text: A rational number is an element of Q, the field of fractions of Z. Concretely, every rational number can be represented as p/q for integers p and nonzero q, with p/q=r/s precisely when ps=rq for nonzero q,s.

context: Infinite sequence: function from N (or positive integers) to Q
editorial_note: The separately sourced Rational Sequence entry specifies rational codomain and the general Sequence entry specifies an index set drawn from N. We must not confuse a rational sequence with a rational-number-valued limit, and finite sequences are not the ones used in the classical rational-Cauchy completion.
text: A rational sequence indexed by the positive integers is a function a:N_{>=1}→Q. Its nth term is a_n=a(n). More generally, a sequence of rational numbers may have a specified subset of N as its index set; the infinite Cauchy construction uses all positive-integer indices.

context: Ordered field Q: modulus using only the rational order and additive inverse
editorial_note: ProofWiki defines absolute value in any ordered integral domain and explicitly lists Q as an instance. Applying the order-based definition to Q remains entirely rational-valued; it must not be replaced by the square-root model for general real numbers. Rational epsilon and rational differences can thus be compared without circularity.
text: For q in Q with its usual total order, the rational absolute value |q| is q if q≥0 and −q if q<0. This gives a function |·|:Q→Q_{≥0} without presupposing real numbers or square roots.

context: Rational order: strictly above zero (ε>0, excluding ε=0)
editorial_note: ProofWiki distinguishes Q_{>0} from its use of 'positive rational number' for Q_{≥0}, which includes zero. Quantifiers in the Cauchy criterion must use strictly positive rational epsilon. The two conventions cannot be conflated or grouped under the same uncontrolled 'positive' variant.
text: A rational number ε is strictly positive if ε>0 in the usual order on Q. The collection of such numbers is Q_{>0}={q in Q:q>0}; zero is excluded.
